keyConcepts.title: The CAP Theorem
keyConcepts.explanation: A distributed data store can simultaneously provide at most two of three guarantees: Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. In real networks, P is mandatory, forcing a trade-off between C and A.

keyConcepts.title: Raft Consensus Protocol
keyConcepts.explanation: A consensus algorithm designed to be understandable, decomposing consensus into leader election, log replication, and safety. A node can be Leader, Follower, or Candidate.

keyConcepts.title: Consistent Hashing
keyConcepts.explanation: Distributes keys across a ring topology using hash ranges with virtual nodes. When nodes join or leave, only K/N keys need to be remapped on average.

keyConcepts.title: Vector Clocks
keyConcepts.explanation: An algorithm for generating a partial ordering of events in a distributed system and detecting causality violations or concurrent conflicts without synchronized physical wall clocks.

definitions.definition: A condition where a distributed cluster divides into two or more independent partitions, each believing it is the sole active cluster.
The strongest consistency model, guaranteeing that all operations appear to execute atomically at a specific point in time between their invocation and response.
Technique in consistent hashing where each physical server maps to multiple tokens across the hash ring to guarantee uniform key distribution.

mainPoints: Network partitions cannot be avoided; systems must explicitly design their failover and degradation modes.
Raft achieves fault tolerance as long as a quorum (strict majority: (N/2)+1) of nodes remains operational.
Eventual consistency guarantees that all replicas will converge given sufficient time without new updates.
Two-Phase Commit (2PC) is a blocking atomic commit protocol, vulnerable if the coordinator crashes during the prepare phase.
revisionHighlights: Quorum formula: Read quorum (R) + Write quorum (W) > Total nodes (N) guarantees strong consistency.
Heartbeat timeout in Raft is typically 150ms-300ms randomized to avoid split votes.
PACELC extends CAP: If there is a Partition, trade Availability vs Consistency; Else, trade Latency vs Consistency.

flashcards.front: What does the CAP Theorem state for networked distributed systems?
flashcards.back: Because physical network partitions (P) are inevitable in real networks, a system can only guarantee either strict Consistency (C) or Availability (A) during network failure, never both.

flashcards.front: What are the three states a node can have in the Raft consensus algorithm?
flashcards.back: Follower (passive, responds to RPCs), Candidate (starts election after heartbeat timeout), and Leader (handles client writes and dispatches AppendEntries RPCs).

flashcards.front: Why does Consistent Hashing use "Virtual Nodes"?
flashcards.back: To prevent "hot spots" and ensure uniform distribution of keys across physical nodes, especially when server hardware capacities differ or the number of physical nodes is small.

flashcards.front: What is the main drawback of the Two-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol?
flashcards.back: It is a blocking protocol. If the coordinator crashes after nodes have acknowledged the "Prepare" phase, participants must wait indefinitely, holding database row locks.

flashcards.front: In Dynamo-style storage, how do R, W, and N relate to strong consistency?
flashcards.back: When R + W > N (where N is replication factor, R is read quorum, and W is write quorum), any read set overlaps with at least one node containing the latest write.

flashcards.front: What does the PACELC theorem add to the CAP theorem?
flashcards.back: If Partition (P), trade Availability (A) vs Consistency (C); Else (E), when running normally, trade Latency (L) vs Consistency (C).

questions.prompt: Under the CAP Theorem, when an unavoidable network partition separates a cluster into two disconnected segments, what must an CP system choose to do?
questions.explanation: In a CP (Consistent & Partition Tolerant) system, nodes on a partition that cannot achieve a verified majority quorum reject incoming writes and reads to avoid split-brain and stale reads, sacrificing availability.

options.text: Accept all writes on both sides and resolve conflicts with timestamps
Reject writes on the minority partition to prevent conflicting updates
Automatically double the replication factor across all alive nodes
Shut down the entire distributed cluster until the physical link recovers

questions.prompt: In the Raft consensus algorithm, how does a candidate node prevent split-vote deadlocks during leader elections?
questions.explanation: Raft uses randomized election timeouts (e.g. 150ms-300ms) for each node so that typically a single follower times out first, increments the term, and collects votes before other nodes wake up.

options.text: By electing the node with the lowest IP address in the cluster
By utilizing randomized election timeouts across nodes
By requiring every candidate to communicate through an external Zookeeper coordinator
By allowing multiple leaders to serve writes concurrently on distinct partitions

questions.prompt: When adding 1 new cache server to a cluster of N existing cache servers using traditional modulo hashing (hash(key) % N), what fraction of keys typically need to be re-cached?
questions.explanation: With standard modulo hashing, changing N to N+1 alters the modulus result for nearly all keys (approx N/(N+1) ≈ 80-90%+ of keys), whereas Consistent Hashing only moves K/(N+1) keys.

options.text: Only 1/N of keys
Almost all keys (approximately N / (N + 1))
Zero keys, because caching is non-deterministic
Exactly 50% of the key space

questions.prompt: In distributed storage systems, what is the purpose of Vector Clocks?
questions.explanation: Vector clocks record the causal history of events across independent processes. By comparing vector clock vectors, the system can determine whether event A happened-before event B or if they are concurrent conflicts.

options.text: To synchronize GPS physical clock time down to microseconds
To detect causal relationships and concurrent update conflicts
To encrypt data packets in transit between data center regions
To calculate the round-trip ping time to client web browsers

questions.prompt: Why is Two-Phase Commit (2PC) considered a blocking protocol in distributed database transactions?
questions.explanation: If the coordinator crashes after participants vote "YES" in Phase 1 (Prepare), participants must hold local locks and cannot unilaterally commit or abort until the coordinator recovers.

options.text: Participants must block because network latency is always non-zero
If the coordinator fails after participants prepare, participants cannot decide independently
It requires locking all DNS records across global regions
It prevents read-only transactions from ever finishing
